claims.text: BCC MoNbTaW can be prepared or represented as a random solid-solution refractory high-entropy alloy.
The disordered MoNbTaW state has high configurational entropy.
Disordered concentrated RHEAs have low lattice thermal conductivity because of mass-disorder scattering.
Mass disorder and random strain fields dominate phonon scattering in the fully disordered baseline state.
Controlled intermediate-temperature processing can induce SRO in MoNbTaW.
SRO can be present in single-phase homogeneous MoNbTaW without long-range ordering.
The relevant SRO consists of B2-like or L12-like local clusters.
These SRO motifs create atomic-scale periodic potential variations distinct from the potential of a random alloy.
The relevant SRO transport regime for RHEAs is typically between 300 K and 1000 K and below the order-disorder transition.
The intrinsic effect of SRO should be evaluated in the absence of significant grain-boundary and precipitate scattering.
SRO may introduce new phonon-scattering channels.
The influence of SRO on phonon scattering depends on the characteristics of the SRO and on the alloy system.
SRO may reduce lattice thermal conductivity relative to the disordered state of the same composition.
The SRO effect on thermal conductivity should be strongest at intermediate temperatures where phonon-phonon scattering is appreciable but not dominant.
At very high temperatures, thermal vibrations may wash out the SRO contribution to phonon scattering.
At low temperatures, matching between the SRO correlation length and phonon wavelength may permit coherent transmission and enhance conductivity.
Low-temperature coherent enhancement is unlikely in RHEAs because they have a broad phonon spectrum.
HEXRD or APT can be used to quantify the SRO parameter in the proposed samples.
TDTR or LFA can be used to determine lattice thermal conductivity in the proposed comparison.
A measured lattice thermal conductivity in the SRO sample that is equal to or higher than that of the disordered sample is defined as falsifying the proposed suppression hypothesis.
